hooks.text: The Moon's surface dust smells like burnt gunpowder.
Why does the Moon smell like burnt gunpowder?
The airless Moon actually smells like spent gunpowder.

title: Why the Moon Smells Like Gunpowder
description: The Moon's abrasive dust levitates under solar radiation and holds a surprising scent. Here is what twelve Apollo astronauts discovered on our nearest neighbor.

beats.text: The Moon's surface dust smells like burnt gunpowder.
beats.visual: Apollo 11 photograph of a bootprint in fine lunar regolith, 1969

beats.text: Solar radiation gives that abrasive dust an electrostatic charge.
beats.visual: Microscopic view of sharp, jagged lunar regolith grains from Apollo samples

beats.text: Instead of resting quietly, the particles actually levitate above the ground.
beats.visual: Artist concept of electrostatic dust levitation above the sunlit lunar horizon

beats.text: A nearly vacuum exosphere leaves the regolith completely exposed to space.
beats.visual: Photograph of the lunar horizon and black sky from Apollo 16, 1972
queries: Moon lunar surface black sky Apollo

beats.text: Down there, surface gravity is only one-sixth of Earth's.

beats.text: NASA's SOFIA airborne observatory detected water across that sunlit surface in October 2020.

beats.text: Across six Apollo missions, exactly twelve humans walked on that ground.
beats.visual: Photograph of Apollo 17 astronaut Harrison Schmitt covered in lunar dust, 1972

beats.text: The only world humans ever visited carries that unmistakable scent.
